 RBI starts new rate-hike cycle as inflation risks mount, raises repo rate to 5.50% 
 RBI starts new rate-hike cycle as inflation risks mount, raises repo rate to 5.50%
 News 
 08 Oct 2026 | Thursday 
 Share: 
 MPC shifts stance to calibrated tightening; GDP growth forecast raised to 7.1 per cent, while CPI inflation forecast climbs to 5.2 per cent, opines Crisil
 The Reserve Bank of India has reopened the rate-hike cycle, raising its policy rate for the first time in more than three years as a deteriorating inflation outlook begins to outweigh an otherwise resilient domestic growth picture. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent at its October 7, 2026 review, marking the first increase since February 2023.
 The move also marks a clear shift in the RBI’s policy direction. The MPC changed its stance to ‘calibrated tightening’ from ‘neutral’, signalling that the central bank is prepared to raise rates further or pause depending on how inflation evolves. The Standing Deposit Facility rate now stands at 5.25 per cent, while the Marginal Standing Facility rate is 5.75 per cent.
 The decision reflects a changing macroeconomic trade-off. Inflation has firmed in recent months, with risks from food, crude oil and other commodities becoming more pronounced, even as domestic activity remains stronger than anticipated. Since the August policy review, oil prices have risen around 40 per cent, while monsoon-related risks have materialised. At the same time, GDP growth surprised on the upside in the first quarter and high-frequency indicators suggest that economic activity remained healthy in July and August.
 The MPC responded by raising its GDP growth forecast for the fiscal by 40 basis points to 7.1 per cent, following better-than-expected first-quarter growth and resilient manufacturing and services activity. GDP grew 7.8 per cent in the first quarter, although the central bank expects some moderation in subsequent quarters.
 The growth trajectory is projected to soften from 7.2 per cent in the second quarter to 6.9 per cent in the third quarter and 6.8 per cent in the fourth quarter, before recovering to 7.1 per cent in the first quarter of the next fiscal. Even with this moderation, growth is expected to remain below the 7.8 per cent recorded in the previous year.
 The inflation picture, meanwhile, has become materially less comfortable. CPI-based inflation rose to 4.8 per cent in August, remaining above the RBI’s 4 per cent target for three consecutive months. The pressure is no longer confined to food and fuel. Core inflation, which represents more than half of the CPI basket, accelerated to 4.2 per cent in August, from around 3.9 per cent in each of the preceding three months, suggesting that higher input costs are increasingly being passed through from producers to consumers.
 The monsoon has added to those concerns. Cumulative southwest monsoon rainfall was 13 per cent below the long-period average at the end of September, the largest deficit recorded since calendar year 2015. As many as 42 per cent of subdivisions recorded deficient rainfall, raising the risk of weaker agricultural output. Likely El Niño conditions add another threat, particularly for Rabi production and rural demand.
 Crude oil has emerged as another significant inflationary risk. Renewed geopolitical uncertainty in West Asia has pushed oil prices above $100 a barrel, compared with $85-90 a barrel at the beginning of August. The roughly 40 per cent increase since the previous policy review raises the prospect of broader cost pressures feeding into the economy.
 Against this backdrop, the MPC raised its CPI inflation forecast by 20 basis points to 5.2 per cent for the fiscal. Inflation is expected to average 4.9 per cent in the second quarter, before peaking at 6.0 per cent in the third quarter. It is then projected to moderate gradually, but remain above the RBI’s target at 5.7 per cent in the fourth quarter and 5.6 per cent in the first quarter of fiscal 2028. Core inflation is expected to average 4.4 per cent during the fiscal.
 The combination of stronger growth and worsening inflation risks explains the timing of the rate action. Domestic demand has remained resilient, while the revival of foreign capital inflows has eased liquidity conditions and supported credit growth. The policy tightening therefore comes at a point when the economy has greater capacity to absorb higher borrowing costs than it might have during a weaker growth cycle.
 The RBI’s rate move is also broadly aligned with the direction of global monetary policy. S&P Global expects the US Federal Reserve to raise policy rates by another 50 basis points during the remainder of 2026, following a 25-basis-point increase in September. The RBI’s shift towards a tighter stance therefore comes as major central banks remain focused on containing inflationary pressures.
 Despite the higher policy rate, credit demand is expected to remain robust. Bank credit growth is projected at 14.5-15.5 per cent this fiscal, reflecting resilient demand for credit and improving economic activity. The rate hike is therefore unlikely to signal an abrupt withdrawal of monetary support; rather, it represents an attempt to prevent emerging inflationary pressures from becoming entrenched while keeping financial conditions orderly.
 Liquidity management is an important part of that adjustment. The RBI has been absorbing substantial excess liquidity from the banking system over the past two months, following a significant inflow of funds, particularly through Foreign Currency Non-Resident Bank (FCNR(B)) deposits.
 In September, the RBI net-absorbed an average Rs 7.8 trillion through the Liquidity Adjustment Facility, more than double the Rs 3.7 trillion absorbed in August. It used two principal instruments: Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) operations and open-market sales of government securities.
 Average VRRR absorption increased to Rs 2.9 trillion in September, from Rs 1.4 trillion in August, while the RBI conducted cumulative Rs 1 trillion of open-market sales of government securities during September. Yet surplus liquidity has not disappeared. The call money rate averaged 5.07 per cent in September, remaining below the 5.50 per cent repo rate, indicating that excess liquidity continues to weigh on short-term market rates.
 The policy combination of a higher repo rate, a tighter stance and active liquidity absorption is therefore aimed at recalibrating financial conditions without disrupting the underlying growth momentum. The immediate challenge for the RBI is to contain the second-round effects of higher food, fuel and commodity costs while avoiding an unnecessary drag on an economy that has continued to outperform expectations.
 The expectation is that the October hike may not be the last. The next policy review will be closely watched for evidence that food supply pressures are easing, crude prices are stabilising and core inflation is responding to tighter financial conditions. A further 25-basis-point rate hike at the December MPC meeting remains a possibility if inflation risks persist.
